title: Anomaly Detection Agent — Database & Endpoint Monitoring with MCP
tagline: An agent that watches your databases and endpoints, then tells you what to fix.
summary: A FastAPI agent that monitors PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MongoDB with read-only connectors, probes backend endpoints for health and response-time regressions, and classifies anomalies — nulls, duplicates, schema violations, slow queries, missing indexes, status-code shifts. Flagged findings go to a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent that writes plain-language explanations with severity, impact, and effort estimates. Ships a React dashboard, a Dockerized stack, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes scans and reports as tools to any MCP client.

caseStudy.problem:
Databases rot silently. Schemas drift, nulls creep in, queries slow down, and endpoints degrade — and teams usually find out from an incident, not a signal. General observability tools raise alerts, but an alert that says 'table scans increased' still leaves a developer to figure out what to do. The brief: a monitoring agent that reads databases and endpoints with read-only access, detects data-quality, performance, and availability anomalies, and hands findings to an LLM agent that produces concrete developer guidance — severity, what broke, and what to fix.

Two design constraints shaped the build: the monitor must never write to a production database (read-only connectors only), and the whole system must run as a demonstrable product without live infrastructure.
requirements: Read-only monitoring of PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MongoDB databases
Endpoint health checks for status-code anomalies, response-time regressions, and timeouts
Detect data-quality issues (nulls, duplicates, schema violations, FK violations) and performance issues (slow queries, missing indexes)
Gemini-powered analysis: human explanations, severity levels, and fix recommendations with impact/effort estimates
REST API to trigger scans and fetch reports
A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing scans and statistics as tools
A dashboard UI and a docker-compose stack
caseStudy.solution:
A four-layer pipeline. The monitor layer (src/monitors) connects to PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MongoDB with read-only queries and probes backend endpoints for availability and latency. The analyzer layer (src/analyzers/detectors.py) classifies signals into data-quality, performance, and endpoint anomalies. The agent layer (src/agents/gemini_agent.py) sends flagged findings to Gemini 2.5 Flash, which returns explanations, severity rankings, and developer recommendations with impact and effort estimates. The API layer (src/api/main.py) persists reports, exposes scan/report endpoints, and feeds the React dashboard.

An MCP server (src/mcp_server.py, FastMCP over stdio) exposes scans, anomaly lists, and statistics as tools any MCP client can call, registered in mcp_config.json. To keep the demo runnable anywhere, the store is in-memory and seeded from mock_data (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB fixtures) via seed_in_memory.py — the same code paths run against real databases when credentials are provided in .env.

architecture.description:
Signals flow forward through the pipeline. Monitors read database schemas and sample data with read-only connectors and probe endpoints; detectors classify the signals into anomalies; the Gemini agent turns those findings into explanations and recommendations; the FastAPI service persists severity-ranked reports and serves them. Two clients consume the service: the React dashboard (reports, stats, scan triggers) and the MCP server, which wraps scans and statistics as tools for any MCP client.

Honest boundary: the MCP tools are currently backed by the seeded in-memory store — the real database connectors are not yet wired into the MCP server, which accepts only the 'mock' scan type. Everything runs from a docker-compose stack, and configuration is environment-driven (Gemini key, database connection strings, scan interval).

caseStudy.implementation:
The monitors (database.py, endpoints.py) execute read-only queries per connector — psycopg2 for PostgreSQL, mysql-connector for MySQL, pymongo for MongoDB — and normalize results into a common signal shape so detectors never care which database produced them. detectors.py runs the rule set: null ratios, duplicate keys, schema-consistency checks, FK violations, slow-query flags, missing-index heuristics, plus HTTP status-code and response-time checks for endpoints. Findings are pushed through gemini_agent.py (google-generativeai, Gemini 2.5 Flash), which returns structured explanations with severity and recommendation fields rendered in the dashboard via react-markdown.

The API (src/api/main.py) exposes POST /api/scan, GET /api/reports, GET /api/reports/{report_id}, POST /api/configure, and GET /api/health; the frontend is a Vite/React SPA with Zustand state, a dashboard with anomaly cards and statistics, a reports page, and an AI chat panel. docker-compose runs API and frontend together, and the seed script loads mock data for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MongoDB fixtures so a full scan works without any live database.

The MCP layer is FastMCP over stdio (scan_anomalies, get_anomalies, get_statistics, clear_anomalies) registered for any client through mcp_config.json — the honest limitation is that scan_anomalies accepts only the 'mock' scan type today, so the real monitors are not yet reachable from MCP.

challenges.title: Three databases, three query dialects, one signal model
challenges.resolution: Per-connector read-only modules that normalize results into a shared shape, so detectors and the agent never see dialect differences.

challenges.title: The demo needed to run with zero live infrastructure
challenges.resolution: An in-memory store seeded from mock_data fixtures for all three databases, so scans and reports work end-to-end anywhere.

challenges.title: The MCP server exposes tools the real monitors aren't wired into
challenges.resolution: Kept honest: scan_anomalies accepts only the 'mock' scan type and tools return the seeded store; the connector wiring is the documented next step rather than pretending it exists.

challenges.title: README promises tests the repo does not ship
challenges.resolution: The pytest command exists but no tests/ directory is committed; the gap is flagged in the lessons below instead of being papered over.

challenges.title: Alerts without context are noise
challenges.resolution: Every anomaly goes through the Gemini agent, which attaches severity, a plain-language explanation, and a concrete fix with effort estimates before it reaches a developer.

lessons: An MCP server is a surface, not a system: the tools here exist and run, but the real connectors aren't wired into them. The scaffold proved the protocol path; the integration is the actual work.
The README promises pytest tests that are not committed — the same trap as other projects: tests must be written and shipped, never promised.
In-memory seeding makes the demo frictionless but hides persistence, scale, and recovery questions; it is a demo strategy, not an architecture.
Read-only monitoring is the right safety default for an agent that touches production databases, and it cost nothing to enforce per connector.
LLM-generated recommendations are only as trustworthy as their evaluation; until the agent's outputs are benchmarked against labeled anomalies, treat them as advisory.
future: Wire the real database and endpoint monitors into the MCP tools and remove the mock-only scan type.
Ship the tests the README claims: detectors, monitors, API, and the MCP tool contracts.

Evaluate Gemini recommendations against labeled anomalies to make severity and fix quality measurable.
